title: Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Water Damage in Galveston?
description: Does homeowners insurance cover water damage? Learn how wind-driven rain, storm surge, and plumbing leaks are treated in Galveston under HO, TWIA and flood.
keyword: does homeowners insurance cover water damage
html:
Does homeowners insurance cover water damage? On Galveston Island, the honest answer is: it depends on where the water came from. Water from a burst pipe, water blown in through a storm-damaged roof, and water that rose from the Gulf or the bay are treated very differently. Many coastal homeowners have three separate policies (a homeowners policy, a TWIA windstorm policy, and a flood policy), and the source of the water decides which one responds. This guide walks through the most common scenarios so you know where to file and what to document.

Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Water Damage? The Three Sources That Matter

Insurers sort water losses by cause. Before you call anyone, figure out which of these describes your loss:

  1. Water from inside the house. A supply line bursts, a water heater fails, an AC drain backs up, or a pipe freezes.
  2. Water from above, driven by wind. Hurricane or storm winds damage the roof, windows or siding, and rain pours in through the opening.
  3. Water from the ground up. Storm surge, tidal flooding, overflow of bayous, or heavy rain that accumulates and enters from below.

Most real hurricane losses in Galveston involve more than one of these at the same time, which is exactly why claims get complicated.

Sudden Plumbing Leaks: Usually a Homeowners Claim

Standard Texas homeowners policies generally cover sudden and accidental discharge of water from plumbing, heating, air conditioning and appliances. That usually includes the damage the water causes to drywall, flooring and cabinets, and often the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to reach the leak.

What is commonly excluded or limited:

  • Long-term, repeated seepage or leakage over weeks or months
  • Wear and tear, rust, and deterioration of the pipe itself
  • Mold, which is often limited or excluded unless tied to a covered water loss
  • Damage made worse because the owner did not take reasonable steps to stop it

Stop the water, take photos and video, call a mitigation company, and keep every invoice. Mold can develop quickly in Galveston humidity, so fast drying protects both your home and your claim.

Wind-Driven Rain: Usually TWIA or Your Wind Coverage

On the coast, many homeowners policies exclude wind and hail, and that coverage is provided by the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) instead. TWIA policies generally cover rain damage to the interior when wind or hail first creates an opening in the roof or walls, such as missing shingles, a torn-off ridge cap, a broken window, or lifted flashing.

That opening is the key fact. If the adjuster concludes rain came in through old cracks, worn flashing or an open window rather than a storm-created opening, the interior water damage may be disputed. So document the opening:

  • Photograph the roof, gutters, and elevations as soon as it is safe
  • Photograph ceiling stains and wet areas directly below the damaged spot
  • Keep debris, such as shingles found in the yard
  • Note the storm date; our weather events log tracks high-wind events in the area
  • Report the claim promptly; TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss

For roof-specific questions, our shingle wind damage calculator shows how different shingle ratings compare to recorded wind speeds, and our TWIA claims help page explains how these claims are handled.

Storm Surge and Flooding: Not Covered by Homeowners or TWIA

This is the one that catches the most people. Homeowners policies and TWIA policies exclude flood. In insurance terms, flood generally includes storm surge, tidal water, overflow of inland or tidal waters, and surface water. If the Gulf or the bay pushes water into your house, that is a flood loss.

Flood damage is covered only if you have a separate flood policy, usually through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) or a private flood insurer. NFIP policies have their own rules, including a proof of loss requirement and limits on what is covered below the lowest elevated floor of elevated homes, which is common on the island. Check your flood declarations page before assuming something is covered.

When Wind and Water Both Hit: Galveston's Biggest Claim Headache

In a hurricane, a Galveston home can take wind damage to the roof and surge damage to the ground floor within hours of each other. Each insurer may try to attribute the damage to the other peril. Common disputes include:

  • Interior ceiling and upper-wall damage (wind-driven rain) versus lower-wall damage (flood)
  • Whether the structure was damaged by wind before the surge arrived
  • Contents that were damaged by both roof leaks and rising water
  • Mold that may have come from either source

The best protection is clear, early documentation showing the high-water line, the roof and envelope damage, and the location of every wet area. Photograph water lines on walls with a tape measure in the shot. Keep separate lists of damage above and below the flood line. File with every insurer that may owe something, and do not let one carrier's denial stop you from pursuing the others.

Quick Reference: Which Policy Might Respond?

  • Burst supply line under the sink: homeowners policy
  • Hurricane tears off shingles and rain soaks the attic: TWIA or wind coverage
  • Storm surge enters the garage and first floor: flood policy
  • Roof leak from old, worn shingles: often denied as wear and tear
  • Fire sprinklers or firefighting water after a fire: typically handled as part of the fire claim; see our Galveston fire claims page

These are general patterns, not guarantees. Your actual policy language controls, so read your declarations, exclusions and endorsements.

Steps to Take After Water Damage in Galveston

  1. Stop the source if you safely can, and shut off power to wet areas.
  2. Photograph and video everything before you move or throw anything away.
  3. Begin drying and mitigation; keep receipts for fans, dehumidifiers, and professional services.
  4. Identify the source of the water and which policies may apply.
  5. Report the claim to each insurer promptly and write down claim numbers.
  6. Request a certified copy of each policy.
  7. Keep samples of damaged materials when practical.
  8. Get an independent repair estimate before accepting a settlement.

Getting Help With a Water Damage Claim

So, does homeowners insurance cover water damage? Sometimes, and when it does not, another policy might. The hard part is proving the cause. A licensed public adjuster (licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance) represents you, not the insurer, and can help document the source of water, separate wind from flood damage, and present the claim to each carrier. faq.q: Does homeowners insurance cover water damage from a hurricane in Galveston?
faq.a: It depends on the source. Rain entering through a wind-created opening is usually a windstorm claim, often with TWIA on the coast. Storm surge and rising water are flood and require a separate flood policy.

faq.q: Is a slow roof leak covered?
faq.a: Often not. Policies commonly exclude long-term leakage, wear and tear, and deterioration. Coverage is more likely when a storm creates a new opening that lets water in.

faq.q: What if my home has both wind and flood damage?
faq.a: File with every insurer that may owe part of the loss, and document the high-water line and roof damage separately. Each carrier pays for the damage caused by its covered peril under its own policy terms.
